key_insight: Instead of training heavy next-frame emulators, learning compact, task-oriented representations of spatiotemporal physical systems yields more efficient, robust solutions for downstream scientific tasks and avoids compounding autoregressive errors.
problem_solved: Current ML workflows focus on next-frame prediction that are costly to train and prone to error accumulation during autoregressive rollouts, making them suboptimal for downstream estimation and analysis tasks in scientific applications.
method: Learn compact latent representations from spatiotemporal data that are explicitly optimized for downstream scientific tasks (e.g., parameter estimation, forecasting of aggregate quantities) rather than pixel-wise next-frame accuracy.
Model short-horizon or latent dynamics in representation space to capture relevant temporal structure without requiring long autoregressive rollouts.
Incorporate task-aligned losses and physics-aware inductive biases to improve robustness, interpretability, and generalization while reducing computational cost.
impact: This shift reduces training and inference cost, mitigates rollout-induced error accumulation, and delivers representations better suited for scientific analysis, enabling faster and more reliable workflows for AI-driven physical modeling.
visual_elements: Side-by-side pipeline diagram: (A) traditional next-frame emulator with long autoregressive rollouts, (B) representation-learning pipeline with encoder → latent → task head.
Schematic of latent-space dynamics showing short-horizon transitions vs long autoregressive sequence to illustrate reduced compounding error.
Bar chart comparing compute/time and downstream task error between emulator-based vs representation-based approaches.
Icons/annotated callouts for benefits: lower compute, better robustness, task alignment, and physics-aware constraints.
paper_title: Representation Learning for Spatiotemporal Physical Systems
paper_authors: Helen Qu, Rudy Morel, Michael McCabe, Alberto Bietti, François Lanusse
